title: Fire Station Living
body:
PURPOSE:
The purpose of this policy is to provide for the health of all members and visitors by establishing guidelines
for fire station cleanliness and maintenance, to ensure that stations and equipment are properly
maintained, and that clean and sanitary conditions exist in the living spaces.
POLICY:
It is the policy of the Stickney Fire Department that routine care, maintenance and cleaning shall be
conducted daily at each station by members on all shifts.
I. PROCEDURE
A. All fire stations and equipment shall be inspected periodically by an Officer in Charge. The
focus of the inspections shall be the proper maintenance and overall cleanliness of the
station and equipment.
B. All members should keep desks, gear lockers, sleeping area, mail boxes, and lockers in a
neat and clean condition. Officers are responsible for monitoring member housekeeping
and hygiene, and immediately addressing any issue that disrupts the good working order
of the station or detracts from a professional image.
C. The station and equipment shall be maintained in a clean, orderly and sanitary condition.
The Stickney Fire Department daily duties and special duties are posted in the day room
and may also be accessed through this policy. (See Daily Duties Section)
D. Additional station and equipment maintenance and cleaning should be conducted weekly
or on an as-needed basis. Sporadic tasks shall be divided between shifts so there is a
shared responsibility for the overall condition of the station and the equipment.
E. Safety considerations regarding cleaning and maintenance may include, but are not
limited to:
1. Cleaning and repairing the source of water leaks quickly to avoid mold growth.
2. Avoiding the use of compressed air to blow dust and debris from the station
uniform or structural firefighting PPE while it is being worn.
3. Maintaining cooking appliances and eating utensils in good working order.
4. Ensuring the hood fan is installed and functioning.
5. Posting signs in all restrooms reminding employees/visitors to wash their hands.

F. All members shall follow established policies and procedures regarding:
1. Beginning and end of shift preparation, readiness, equipment inventory and
testing.
2. Meal plans for the shift.
3. Shift change
4. Permissible and restricted activities and hours.
5. Use of technology and electronics on-duty
G. The Officer or acting Officer shall use the following as an established hierarchy for
conducting a shift:
1. Call response.
2. Apparatus and equipment checks
3. Meals
4. Daily duties.
5. Specialized duties, or those assigned by an Officer.
6. Shift training.
7. Personal time.
H. Any disputes shall be resolved by a supervisor.
II. GROCERY SHOPPING ON DUTY
A. It is the policy of the Stickney Fire Department to encourage suppression personnel to
bring an adequate supply of food to work to meet their nutrition needs for the hours to
be worked. When circumstances allow, companies may be permitted to shop for
groceries as well.
B. Company grocery shopping may be permitted under the following circumstances:
1. All companies shopping for groceries shall remain in service.
2. Companies choosing to grocery shop while on-duty shall make an effort to
incorporate shopping as a part of the daily routine to avoid making a separate
trip.
3. Companies shall shop within their initial response area or at the closest store
approved by the Officer in Charge.
4. Members entering the store shall take a portable radio and if dispatched to a call
shall leave the store immediately.
5. Except for groceries, under the conditions noted in this policy, personal shopping
while on-duty is not permitted.
6. Use of a personal vehicle for grocery shopping while on-duty is not authorized.
7. One crew member shall remain with the unit at all times for apparatus security,
response readiness and public/community outreach.
8. Apparatus shall not be parked in red zones, along red curbs, in zones limited
exclusively to the vehicles of disabled persons or any location that will restrict
pedestrian or vehicular traffic.

III. DAILY DUTIES
A. The following tasks will be completed daily. The officer or acting officer will be
accountable for the completion of the daily duties.
B. MORNINGS
1. Daily vehicle checks for maintenance and equipment will be completed with
corresponding vehicle book filled out
2. Run saws and generators
3. Vacuum all carpeted areas and rugs, including offices
4. Empty all trash cans and recycling can in common areas and offices
5. Empty dishwasher and put away dishes
C. AFTERNOONS
1. Disinfect, sweep, mop, and empty garbage from both the men’s and women’s
bathroom
2. Kitchen countertops and hard surfaces will be free of food debris and disinfected
3. Kitchen sink will be free from dishes, food debris, and be scrubbed clean
4. Hallways, foyer, and kitchen will be swept free of debris and mopped
5. Rubber mats will be replaced after mopping and the floor is dry
6. Bunkroom will be cleaned of all debris
D. NIGHTS
1. Area of ice machine and daily check books will be cleaned of all debris
2. Kitchen countertops and hard surfaces will be free from food debris and
disinfected
3. Kitchen sink will be free from dishes, food debris, and scrubbed clean
E. MONDAY
1. Morning: Weekly checks on 1201
2. Afternoon: Weekly checks on 1208, 1209, and 1210
3. Night: Sweep/remove debris under gear lockers. Wash apparatus floor.
F. TUESDAY
1. Morning: Weekly checks on 1202
2. Afternoon: Weekly checks on 1205. Complete disinfection of all equipment and
vehicle.
3. Night: Clean laundry room. Wash all towels/linen. Clean hose tower, roll any
hanging hose
G. WEDNESDAY
1. Morning: Remove chairs for drill and wipe down tables with disinfectant. Clean
white board
2. Afternoon: Weekly check on 1207. Complete disinfection of all equipment and
vehicle
3. Night: Place chairs on table and vacuum training room

H. THURSDAY
1. Morning: Weekly checks on 1203
2. Afternoon: Interior and exterior cleaning of all fire house windows
3. Night: Sweep/remove debris under gear lockers. Wash apparatus floor
I. FRIDAY
1. Morning: Weekly checks on 1204
2. Afternoon: Scrub floor in men’s and women’s bathroom with soap and hard floor
brushes. Wash shower curtains
3. Night: Straighten, disinfect, and mop weight room, second floor, and stairwell
J. SATURDAY
1. Morning: Clean grill. Clean exterior patio area and perimeter of firehouse of
garbage and debris
2. Afternoon: Complete cleaning of kitchen and pantry. Grease traps emptied. Pull
out fridge, freezer, and stove to sweep and mop behind them. Scrub debris from
floor. Fridge cleaned out of old food and shelves disinfected. Stove grates
removed and scrubbed. All surface areas cleaned and disinfected.
3. Night: Service cascade system.
K. SUNDAY
1. Morning: Inventory and wash light tower. Light tower will be started and ran with
lights on the 1st Sunday morning of every month
2. Afternoon/Night: Complete cleaning of bunkroom. Vacuum, hard surface
disinfection, and remove debris. Mattress covers will be washed.
IV. WEEKLY VEHICLE CHECKS
A. Inventory all equipment on vehicle, report missing equipment
B. Perform SCBA checks and record
C. Complete maintenance on vehicle and record
D. Run all applicable equipment on the vehicle
1. All extrication equipment, jaws, cutter, airbags, etc.
2. Saws and power tools
3. Pump
E. Wash vehicle exterior
F. Clean, sweep/vacuum vehicle interior of gross debris
G. Disinfect vehicle interior passenger area (all vehicles except 1210)
H. Clean interior windows
I. Change radio batteries
J. Fuel vehicle
K. VEHICLE WAXING
1. Vehicle waxing will be completed during the first week of vehicle checks in the
months of April and September

2. Completion of vehicle waxing will be indicated on the designated vehicle white
board
3. Any vehicle waxing unable to be completed as scheduled will be passed on, by
the officer or acting officer, to the oncoming officer or acting officer
V. SNOW REMOVAL
A. Snow removal and salting will be completed by every shift as needed whenever snow fall
covers the paved/cement areas of the fire station.
B. During continuous snowfall, snow removal and salting will be performed a minimum of
once per shift, or more as determined by the officer or acting officer for the following
areas:
1. Entire sidewalk along 43rd St. parking strip
2. Fire station front walkway, all cemented area
3. Fire station front apron
4. Fire station rear apron
5. Handicapped parking spaces
6. Fire station rear entrance
7. Fire station side entrance
By Order of:
Jeff Boyajian
Fire Chief

title: Shift Exchange And Coverage
body:
PURPOSE:
This policy describes the department's expectations of its employees when obtaining shift coverage or
engaging in shift trades for assigned duty hour to ensure the continued ability of the Stickney Fire
Department to carry out its mission and duties.
POLICY:
It is the policy of this department to identify the expectations required of its members when obtaining
shift trades or shift coverage for assigned duty hours in order to provide efficient and quality services to
the community and to promote the efficient operation of the Stickney Fire Department.
I. SHIFT EXCHANGE
A. Members are required to request permission for a shift exchange 72 hours in advance of
the duty hours to be worked.
B. The Aladtec scheduling software will be used to submit all scheduling trades.
By Order of:
Jeff Boyajian
Fire Chief

title: Incident Management
body:
PURPOSE:
The purpose of this policy is to establish operational guidelines for members of the Department to use in
the management and mitigation of all-hazards emergency incidents.
POLICY:
It is the policy of the Stickney Fire Department to utilize the Incident Command System (ICS) or other
National Incident Management System (NIMS)-compliant incident management system for managing all
emergency incidents. All incident-related activities should be managed in accordance with established
ICS/NIMS methods and procedures.
It is the policy of this department that supervisors periodically account for members working under their
direction at emergency incidents and that all members participate in accountability systems.
I. DEFINITIONS
A. All-hazards - An incident, natural or manmade, that warrants action to protect life,
property, the environment, and public health or safety, and to minimize disruptions of
government, social or economic activities.
B. Personnel Accountability Report (PAR) - A roll call of all operations members assigned to
an incident at specified times; a PAR is designed to account for each member’s location
and activity and to verify his/her safety.
II. INCIDENT MANAGEMENT
A. The Fire Chief shall ensure the Department adopts written ICS/NIMS procedures that are
compatible with neighboring jurisdictions. These procedures will be available to members
and incorporated into departmental training.
B. Emergency incidents shall be managed utilizing trained and qualified personnel for the
specific tactical, supervisory or command level assignments.
III. INCIDENT COMMAND
A. The purpose of Incident Command is to have a formal procedure to readily implement
the Incident Command System on emergency incidents and to establish formal guidelines
to be utilized by individuals with responsibilities associated with emergency incident risk
management analysis and personnel resource management.

B. Every emergency incident situation requires that an individual assume responsibility for
developing strategic objectives and a tactical action plan. Critical to the development of
the strategy and implementation of the tactical plan is an accurate assessment of the level
of potential risk that responders and potential victims may be subjected to based upon
present and potentially deteriorating conditions.
C. Emergency incident safety is paramount with respect to decisions related to deployment
of personnel resources. Toward that objective these guidelines reflect accepted practices
outlined in NFPA 1500 “Fire Department Occupational Safety and Health Program,”
Chapter Six, Emergency Operations.
IV. RISK MANAGEMENT DURING EMERGENCY OPERATIONS
A. The Incident Commander shall integrate risk management into the regular functions of
Incident Command and in so doing shall base risk management on the following
principles:
B. Priorities in the deployment of personnel resources at an emergency incident must be
consistent with the following principles.
1. Activities that present a significant risk (i.e.: death, serious injury, etc.) to the
safety of personnel shall be limited to situations where there is a potential to save
endangered lives.
2. Activities that are routinely employed to protect property shall be recognized as
inherent risks (heat, potential rapid fire spread, structural instability, etc.) to the
safety of personnel, and actions shall be taken to reduce or avoid these risks.
3. No undue risk to the safety of members shall be acceptable when there is no
possibility to save lives or significant property of value.
C. If the I.C (typically the On-duty Firefighter until relieved by incoming officer) in charge has
any doubt concerning the capability of on-scene resources to safely conduct interior
operations without undue reasonable risks (large volume fire, impending structural
collapse, haz-mat presence, etc.) to personnel, as defined above, defense operations
should be the course of action until arrival of additional resources. It must be recognized
that every situation is unique and that an all-encompassing definition for undue risk is
impossible. The ability for the I.C. to use discretion on a situation specific basis is very
important. It is not the intent of this policy to mandate how an I.C. will react in every
situation.
D. Personnel Operating at Emergency Incidents: Initial Stage Operations Once a decision has
been made identifying the level of risk present for a specific emergency incident, the I.C.
must determine how and where available personnel resources will be deployed
considering: 1) safety of personnel relative to risk; and 2) strategic objectives and tactical
plan.
E. The Stickney Fire Department shall provide an adequate number of personnel to safely
conduct emergency scene operations (NFPA 1500, 6-4.1).
F. In the initial stages of an incident (tasks undertaken by first arriving engine company)
where only one team is operating in the hazardous area, at least one additional member
shall be assigned to stand by outside of the hazardous area where the team is operating
(NFPA 1500, 6-4.4).

G. Standby member shall be responsible for maintaining a constant awareness of the
number and identity of personnel operating in the hazardous area, their location and
function, and time of entry. Standby member shall also remain in radio, visual, voice or
signal line communications with the team (NFPA 1500, 6-4.4). (Standby member can also
be the pump operator).
H. If, after evaluating the risk, personnel are going to initiate actions that would involve
entering a structure to prevent loss of life, serious injury, or significant valuable property,
and a second team is not at the scene, incoming companies shall be notified so that they
will be prepared to provide necessary support and backup upon their arrival (NFPA 1500,
A-6-4.1.1).
V. FIREGROUND ACCOUNTABILITY
A. The purpose of this policy is to increase firefighter safety by establishing accountability
systems for keeping track of all personnel operating at the scene of an emergency
incident.
B. A personnel accountability system shall be established and implemented using thorough
training procedures. This system should constantly monitor the status of all emergency
personnel, both of department members and personnel from assisting agencies, during
emergency incidents from their arrival until their official release from the incident.
C. A personnel accountability system should be used primarily to track personnel, not
resources. However, on small incidents one individual may be responsible for tracking
both personnel and resources.
D. A written personnel accountability system, such as the Incident Command System (ICS)
Form I-201 for Incident Commanders (IC) or some similar process, a status board, helmet
shields, passports and name tags should be maintained. Individual crew names shall be
posted in a conspicuous location in the cab of department vehicles.
E. Supervisors are responsible for participation in the accountability system by tracking all
personnel under their direction on emergency incidents. Personnel should be accounted
for from the time of dispatch to the time of demobilization.
F. Supervisors should implement sufficient tracking methods for personnel at the individual,
company, division, group and unit levels to account for personnel during all phases and
at all locations of an incident, including travel between locations and assignments.
G. The IC should designate an accountability officer to monitor who is in charge of each area,
what crews are assigned to each area, where each area is located and the area
assignment.
H. Division or sector supervisors should be assigned to keep track of all crews under their
supervision. Company Officers should know the location and assignment of each
firefighter in their crew.
I. All members are responsible for participating in the accountability system, including
checking in at approved locations. This includes members who arrive on-scene
individually or in privately owned vehicles.

VI. REPORTING
A. Ongoing, routine strategic and tactical accountability at all emergency incidents, including
wildland fires, should be accomplished through periodic reporting or visual observation.
B. This can be accomplished through concise reports that include conditions, actions and
needs, also called a CAN report. Members should also make the following reports:
1. Emergency situations
2. Inability to meet objective with revised timeline and/or resource requests
3. Notification of completed actions
4. Change in strategy
5. Change in fire conditions
C. 302.4.1 PERSONNEL ACCOUNTABILITY REPORTS (PAR)
1. For structure fires, a PAR should be conducted within the first 10 minutes of an
incident and every 20 minutes thereafter for personnel at the scene. In addition,
PARs should be conducted after any change in conditions that may alter or affect
firefighter safety, such as a change in fire conditions, a change in strategy, or after
ordering an emergency evacuation of an area.
2. A PAR should be conducted for each division, sector and organizational element
where operations personnel are working. If any person involved in the operation
is unaccounted for, emergency procedures, including notification to the IC should
be initiated.
3. The IC may discontinue regular PARs when incident stabilization is achieved, and
hazards are sufficiently reduced.
By Order of:
Jeff Boyajian
Fire Chief

title: Emergency Response
body:
PURPOSE:
The purpose of this policy is to ensure a safe and appropriate response to emergencies while maintaining
the safety of department members and the public by requiring operators of department vehicles to
conform to applicable Illinois laws and regulations during an emergency response.
The purpose of this policy is to establish turnout, travel and response time goals and objectives for
emergency incidents for the Stickney Fire Department.
POLICY:
It is the policy of the Stickney Fire Department to appropriately respond to all emergency calls. It is the
policy of the Stickney Fire Department to document all of the response times to emergency incidents and
establish response time baselines and performance objectives.
I. DEFINITIONS
A. Authorized emergency vehicle - Department vehicles of the fire department as authorized
by 625 ILCS 5/1-105.
B. Emergency response - Any call for service or assistance involving fire, explosion, or violent
rupture; human rescue; human entrapment; illness or injury; hazardous materials release
or threat of contamination; flooding; threatened or actual acts of violence; any explosive,
bomb, or threatened bombing; any act of terrorism; any natural disaster; or any other
circumstance that presents a threat to life-safety or to property.
C. Dispatch processing time - The time elapsed between receipt of the alarm or telephone
call and the dispatch of emergency response units.
D. Response time - The time elapsed between the dispatch center receiving the first
notification of the alarm and the arrival of the first emergency response unit. Response
time combines dispatch processing, turnout, and travel times.
E. Travel time - The time elapsed between the emergency response unit beginning travel to
the emergency and when the emergency response unit arrives.
F. Turnout time - The time elapsed between Dispatch notifying members of the Stickney Fire
Department of the emergency and when the emergency response unit begins travel.

II. EMERGENCY CALLS
A. Fire personnel dispatched to an emergency shall proceed immediately, shall continuously
operate emergency lighting equipment and shall sound the siren as reasonably necessary
(625 ILCS 5/12-601(b)).
B. Responding with emergency lights and siren does not relieve personnel of the duty to
continue to drive with due regard for the safety of all persons or protect the driver from
the consequences of his/her reckless disregard for the safety of others (625 ILCS 5/11-
205(e)).
C. Personnel should only respond with emergency lights and siren when dispatched to an
emergency or when circumstances reasonably indicate an emergency response is
required.
D. Personnel not responding with emergency lights and siren shall observe all traffic laws
and proceed without the use of emergency lights and siren.
III. MULTIPLE EMERGENCY VEHICLE RESPONSES
A. When more than one apparatus responds to an emergency, emergency vehicle operators
should remain alert to the presence of other emergency vehicles and exercise due
caution.
B. Personnel must further exercise due caution in recognizing that traffic yielding to one
emergency vehicle may not expect other emergency vehicles to follow.
IV. INITIATING AN EMERGENCY RESPONSE
A. Notification of an emergency call will be given to the on-duty crew through the dispatch
agency.
B. It is the discretion of the Officer in Charge to deviate from this practice for calls received
directly on a Stickney Fire Department phone line.
V. RESPONSIBILITIES OF RESPONDING PERSONNEL
A. Authorized emergency vehicle operators shall exercise sound judgment and care, with
due regard for life and property, while operating a vehicle enroute to an emergency
response.
B. In addition, emergency vehicle operators should reduce speed at all street intersections
and should come to a complete stop at all blind street intersections or intersections where
there is either a red light, a flashing red light, or a stop sign. Emergency vehicle operators
should also come to a complete stop at intersections whenever they reasonably believe
they cannot account for traffic in approaching lanes or when vehicles have not yielded
the right-of-way. After coming to a complete stop, emergency vehicle operators should
only proceed when it is safe to do so.
C. During a response to an emergency call, the driver of an authorized emergency vehicle
may, with lights and sirens activated (625 ILCS 5/11-205(c)(d)):
1. Park or stand.
2. Exceed the maximum speed limit so long as the driver does not endanger life or
property.
3. Disregard regulations governing direction of movement or turning in specified
directions.

D. The decision to continue an emergency response is at the discretion of the authorized
emergency vehicle operator or Officer in charge. If, in the judgment of either individual,
the roadway conditions or traffic congestion do not permit such a response without
unreasonable risk, the response may be continued without the use of red lights and siren
and at the legal speed limit. In such an event, the Officer in charge should ensure Dispatch
is promptly notified. Personnel shall also discontinue the emergency response when
directed by any supervisor.
VI. FAILURE OF EMERGENCY EQUIPMENT
A. If the emergency equipment on the vehicle should fail to operate, the vehicle operator
must terminate the emergency response and respond accordingly.
B. In all cases, the Officer in charge shall notify Dispatch of the equipment failure so that
another apparatus may be assigned to the emergency response.
VII. RESPONSE TIME STANDARDS
A. Response times should be measured at 90 percent of fractal time and reported against
an established department Stickney Fire Department Standards of Cover document, if
available.
B. Performance objectives may include:
1. One minute or less for dispatch processing time.
2. One minute or less for turnout time for Emergency Medical Services (EMS)
incidents.
3. One minute 20 seconds or less for turnout time for non-EMS incidents.
4. Four minutes or less for the arrival of the first engine company at a fire
suppression incident.
5. Eight minutes or less for the arrival of a full first-alarm assignment at a fire
suppression incident.
6. Four minutes or less for the arrival of a unit with Emergency Medical Responder
(EMR) or higher level capability at an emergency medical incident.
7. Eight minutes or less for the arrival of an advanced life support (ALS) unit at an
emergency medical incident when this service is provided by the Department
Stickney Fire Department.
C. EVALUATIONS AND ANNUAL REPORT
1. The Department Stickney Fire Department shall annually evaluate its level of
service, deployment delivery and response time objectives.
2. The evaluation shall be based on data relating to level of service, deployment,
and the achievement of each response time performance objective in the
geographic area of the jurisdiction.
By Order of:
Jeff Boyajian
Fire Chief

title: Fire Investigations
body:
PURPOSE:
The purpose of this policy is to ensure that all fires and explosions responded to by the Stickney Fire
Department and occurring within this jurisdiction are investigated and properly documented in
accordance with state and federal laws as well as national standards.
POLICY:
It is the policy of the Stickney Fire Department to promptly investigate the cause, origin, and
circumstances of fires and explosions occurring in this jurisdiction that involve the loss of life or injury to
a person, or the destruction of or damage to property.
I. RESPONSIBILITIES
A. The Fire Chief has overall responsibility for fire investigations. The Chief of Fire Prevention
is responsible for management of the fire investigations program.
B. The Incident Commander (IC) of each incident is responsible for ensuring that each fire is
investigated for origin and cause.
C. Per State Requirements, all fires involving property destruction or damage will be
investigated. The investigation shall commence within two days, not including Sunday
(425 ILCS 25/6).
II. REPORTS
A. INCIDENT REPORTS
1. To ensure department incidents are documented in the National Fire Incident
Reporting System (NFIRS), investigators should complete and submit a report to
the Chief of Fire Prevention for each investigation conducted. All areas of the
report are to be filled out and when an item is not applicable, N/A is to be placed
in the box. For additional information, see the National Fire Incident Reporting
System (NFIRS) Policy.
2. The Chief of Fire Prevention is responsible for reviewing and approving the
investigative reports.

B. REPORTS TO THE OFFICE OF THE STATE FIRE MARSHAL
1. The Stickney Fire Department shall furnish the OSFM with a statement of facts
relating to the cause and origin of any fire where property was destroyed or
damaged.
2. The statement shall be provided by the 15th of the month following the fire and
be in an approved format or on forms provided by the OSFM (425 ILCS 25/6).
III. PRELIMINARY INVESTIGATION
A. The first-in Company Officer should conduct a preliminary investigation of each fire or
explosion to identify the origin, cause, and circumstances. The Company Officer will notify
the IC of the results of the preliminary investigation.
B. If the origin of a fire or explosion appears to be suspicious, the IC should take immediate
charge of all physical evidence relating to the fire or explosion, coordinate with
investigators, and contact local law enforcement.
C. The IC is responsible for determining when fire investigators, fire investigators with arrest
authority, or sworn law enforcement investigators, from this or another agency, are
appropriate to investigate an incident. The IC will also make the determination of whether
to request a MABAS Division 11 Fire Investigators Box Alarm.
D. The immediate response of an appropriate investigator should be requested when any of
the following circumstances exist:
1. Major or unusual fires that exceed the investigative abilities of a Company Officer
2. Any fire resulting in a major injury or death
3. Incidents involving special circumstances, such as an especially high dollar loss,
extensive damage, political sensitivity, or any other circumstance deemed
appropriate by the Officer in Charge
4. Arson and/or incendiary devices are involved, or the origin of the fire is otherwise
suspicious
5. There has been an explosion
6. There is evidence or suspicion that a crime has occurred in connection with a fire
or explosion
7. A fire has been started by a juvenile
8. Any illegal activity that potentially could cause a fire and/or explosion has
occurred
IV. EQUIPMENT
A. The Division 11 fire investigator's vehicle should be requested as needed and will supply
the following equipment to help investigate fire cause, origin, and circumstance:
1. Digital camera
2. Spare batteries
3. Voice recording device and spare media

4. Fire investigator toolbox
5. Shovels, rake, broom, and sifter
6. Disposable latex evidence collection gloves
7. Evidence collection markers and labels for canisters
B. PROTECTIVE GEAR
1. Fire investigators are responsible for using personal protective equipment (PPE)
and respiratory protection appropriate for the conditions present at an
investigation scene.
2. When entering any fire scene during the fire, before or during overhaul, or when
there is a chance of reignition, fire investigators shall wear full structural PPE and
self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA).
3. See the Respiratory Protection Program Policy and the Personal Protective
Equipment Policy for additional guidance.
V. LOGBOOK
A. Each investigator should maintain a logbook of field training, continued professional
training hours, and investigative experience.
B. The purpose of this log is to assist in establishing the member as an expert witness in
court appearances.
VI. FIRE INVESTIGATORS
A. Fire investigators assigned to an incident are responsible for pursuing the investigation
through its completion and providing complete written documentation.
B. In cases where a fire investigator reasonably believes that arson or an unlawful act may
be involved in a fire, the investigator should consult with the Chief of Fire Prevention and
request the assistance of an investigator with arrest authority, if appropriate.
C. Fire Investigator Qualifications include:
1. Meet the job performance requirements of the National Fire Protection
Association’s (NFPA) standards for fire investigators.
2. Complete the certification requirements of the Division of Personnel Standards
and Education.
3. Comply with all federal and state statutory and constitutional investigatory
requirements, including limitations on searches and seizures.
D. FIRE INVESTIGATORS WITH ARREST AUTHORITY
1. Fire investigators with arrest authority assigned to an incident are responsible for
conducting a thorough investigation and providing complete written
documentation.
2. Fire investigators who reasonably anticipate an arrest in connection with an
investigation should arrange to have a law enforcement officer from a law
enforcement agency with jurisdiction present. If a law enforcement officer is
unavailable to assist with an arrest, investigators should delay the arrest until
such time that law enforcement can be present, if possible.

3. In situations where a fire investigator finds it necessary to arrest a suspect
without the assistance of local law enforcement, the investigator shall notify the
local law enforcement agency that an arrest is being made and have another
investigator from this department present on the scene at the time of arrest. Fire
investigators will not make arrests alone, unless exigent circumstances exist.
By Order of:
Jeff Boyajian
Fire Chief

title: Rapid Intervention Two-In Two-Out
body:
PURPOSE:
The purpose of this policy is to increase firefighter safety by implementing procedures for safeguarding
and rescuing firefighters who are operating in environments that are immediately dangerous to life and
health (IDLH).
This policy applies to all members assigned to an incident and is designed to ensure immediate assistance
for members who become lost, trapped or injured by adhering to the two-in/two-out standard and
designating a rapid intervention team (RITs) (820 ILCS 219/25; 29 CFR 1910.134(g) (4)).
POLICY:
It is the policy of the Stickney Fire Department to ensure that adequate personnel are on-scene before
interior operations begin in any IDLH environment. However, nothing in this policy is meant to preclude
firefighters from performing emergency rescue activities before an entire team has assembled.
I. DEFINITIONS
A. Immediately dangerous to life and health (IDLH) - Any atmosphere that poses an
immediate threat to life, would cause irreversible adverse health effects or would impair
an individual’s ability to escape from a dangerous atmosphere. Interior atmospheric
conditions at structure fires beyond the incipient stage are considered IDLH, as are a
variety of rescue types.
B. Mayday - The nationally adopted “call for help” term used to indicate that an emergency
responder is in a situation of imminent peril where he/she is in need of immediate help.
C. Rapid intervention team (RIT) - A formalized designated team of individuals or companies
whose sole function is to prepare, monitor and provide for effective emergency rescue of
responders in IDLH atmospheres.
II. DEPLOYMENT
A. PRE-DEPLOYMENT
1. Prior to initiating any fire attack in any IDLH environment with no confirmed
rescue in progress, members shall ensure that there are sufficient resources onscene to establish two-in/two-out procedures (29 CFR 1910.134(g)(4)).
2. Members shall ensure that at least two firefighters using self-contained breathing
apparatus (SCBA) enter the IDLH environment and remain in voice or visual
contact with one another at all times.

3. At least two additional firefighters shall be located outside the IDLH environment.
4. One of the two outside firefighters may be assigned to an additional role so long
as the individual is able to perform assistance or rescue activities without
jeopardizing the safety or health of any firefighter working at the incident.
B. INITIAL DEPLOYMENT
1. During the initial phase of an incident, confirmed rescues should take priority.
When a confirmed rescue is identified during the initial phase of an incident,
emergency rescue activities may be performed before a designated RIT has
assembled.
2. All members operating in IDLH environments shall be tracked and accounted for
at all times, except when it would preclude firefighters from performing
emergency rescue activities during the initial phase of the incident.
III. RIT DUTIES
A. The RIT should be assembled from resources at the scene, whose sole function is to
prepare for, monitor and provide effective emergency rescue for responders.
1. To the extent possible, visual and voice communication should be maintained
between those working in the IDLH environment and the RIT outside the IDLH
environment.
2. RIT members should not be involved in any other duties that divert attention or
resources away from their primary mission of responder rescue.
3. Additional companies may be assigned to the RIT as conditions warrant. For large
incidents with multiple points of entry, multiple RITs should be considered.
B. EMERGENCY DEPLOYMENT OF A RIT
1. When a Mayday firefighter-down or firefighter-missing broadcast is transmitted,
all non-emergency radio traffic should be cleared from the radio channels that
the missing or trapped firefighter is using. Non-affected personnel should switch
to other tactical frequencies. At least two individuals should be dedicated solely
to monitoring the tactical channel. One person should be responsible for
gathering information on the identity, location and condition of the trapped or
missing firefighter, while the second person should communicate with the
trapped or missing firefighter and offer support on the tactical channel.
2. Additionally, and in keeping with Illinois Mutual Aid Box Alarm System (MABAS)
policy, a Mayday shall be utilized whenever there is:
a) A firefighter injured and in need of immediate assistance.
b) A firefighter lost or missing.
c) A firefighter trapped.
d) A firefighter out of air.
e) A circumstance that can seriously injure a firefighter.
f) A circumstance in which a firefighter locates another firefighter in any of
the above noted situations.

3. For an emergency deployment of a RIT, a RIT Chief position should be activated
to coordinate the rescue as well as any fire activities in support of the rescue
effort. Other divisions and groups may support the RIT Chief's efforts by diverting
fire spread through horizontal or vertical ventilation to draw fire away from the
affected rescue areas and by placing hose streams to check fire spread and
protect rescue efforts.
4. The RIT officer should notify the RIT Chief before making entry for emergency
rescue. The RIT Chief should provide any assistance that is appropriate to the
situation. Additional resources should be ordered as needed, including additional
RITs, medical treatment and transportation groups or other organizational
elements.
By Order of:
Jeff Boyajian
Fire Chief

title: Urban Search And Rescue (USAR)
body:
PURPOSE:
The purpose of this policy is to describe the Illinois Mutual Aid Box Alarm System (MABAS) for requesting
state USAR resources and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Urban Search and Rescue
(USAR) Response System as resources for disaster response. This policy also provides guidelines for the
request and activation of USAR resources for department- involved incidents.
POLICY:
It is the policy of the Stickney Fire Department to utilize the USAR resources coordinated by MABAS and/or
FEMA in the event of an urban disaster, as appropriate.
I. RESOURCES
A. USAR is a multi-hazard discipline and may be used for a variety of disasters, including
hurricanes, earthquakes, typhoons, storms, tornadoes, floods, dam failures, technological
accidents, terrorist activities and hazardous material releases.
B. USAR task forces have four areas of specialization:
1. Searches - Finding victims who are trapped after a disaster
2. Rescues - Freeing victims, including safely digging victims out of collapsed
concrete or metal
3. Technical - Applying specialized structural knowledge to help make rescues safe
for the rescuers
4. Medical - Caring for victims before and after a rescue
C. If a disaster warrants, both MABAS coordinated resources and FEMA resources may be
available for assistance.
II. STATE RESOURCES
A. Local fire departments throughout Illinois presently participate in regional teams. Some
local fire departments own and maintain USAR equipment. MABAS owns and maintains
USAR equipment and trained personnel that can be used throughout the state of Illinois.
B. Local fire departments can request MABAS resources through the MABAS Division
Dispatch Centers. Following a State of Illinois Declaration of Disaster, the Illinois
Emergency Management Agency (IEMA) can activate additional MABAS USAR resources
including IL US&R TF-1, also known as a “Heavy Team,” which is a Type I team modeled
after FEMA USAR teams. (See Appendix A - link to IEMA document)

III. NATIONAL RESOURCES
A. If national USAR support is warranted, IEMA can request FEMA USAR resources. FEMA
may deploy multiple task forces within six hours of notification and can provide additional
teams as necessary to support the Stickney Fire Department’s efforts to locate victims
and manage recovery operations.
B. The following resources are generally available from the FEMA USAR Response System:
1. Air Search Team (fixed-wing)
2. Airborne Reconnaissance (fixed-wing)
3. Canine - Avalanche/Snow
4. Canine - Disaster Response
5. Canine - Land/Cadaver
6. Canine - Water
7. Canine - Wilderness
8. Canine - Wilderness Tracking and Trailing
9. Cave Search and Rescue Team
10. Collapse Search and Rescue Team
11. Mine and Tunnel Search and Rescue Team
12. Mountain Search and Rescue Team
13. Radio Direction Finding Team
14. Swiftwater and Flood Search, and Dive Rescue Team
15. USAR Incident Support Team
16. USAR Task Force
17. Wilderness Search and Rescue Team
C. More information about the specific capabilities and sustainability of federal USAR
resources may be obtained on the FEMA website. ( https://www.fema.gov/emergencymanagers/national-preparedness/frameworks/urban-search-rescue )
By Order of:
Jeff Boyajian
Fire Chief
Appendix A – IEMA Urban Search and Rescue

title: Tactical Withdrawal
body:
PURPOSE:
The purpose of this policy is to establish guidelines for tactical withdrawals from any scene or location
when confronted by violent individuals or threatening situations, circumstances or events. The violence
or threat need not be specifically directed at department members to justify the application of this policy.
POLICY:
The Stickney Fire Department is committed to the safety of its members. It is the policy of the Stickney
Fire Department to allow members to withdraw from the scene or general location of an emergency call
for service when they are confronted by violent individuals, violent or potentially violent situations or any
other circumstance presenting a real or perceived imminent threat to member safety.
I. THREAT ASSESSMENT
A. All members of the Department are expected to continually evaluate their surroundings
while responding to incidents or participating in the mitigation of emergency or nonemergency events. The actions and conduct of persons at an event should be a primary
element of the ongoing scene- safety evaluation. Certain types of events, certain actions
taken by individuals involved in events and a variety of other circumstances should trigger
a heightened awareness and consideration of personnel safety. Situations or
circumstances that shall initiate such consideration include:
1. Gang-related activity, particularly any event involving violent encounters,
confrontations or conflicts between members of rival gangs.
2. Any situation involving shots fired, or on any scene where shooting occurs or is
heard in the immediate vicinity.
3. Any time a subject challenges or threatens members of the Department with
violence or harm.
4. Any scene where members of the Department are attacked in any way. Examples
include rocks, bottles or other projectiles thrown or launched at members or
department vehicles or apparatus; individuals attempting to gain access to
department vehicles or apparatus; or any direct act of violence committed
against members of this department.

5. Any event involving civil disturbance, large-scale demonstrations or protests. This
includes any event involving a large gathering of people where the nature of the
activity appears to include violent confrontation or the perceived threat of violent
confrontation between opposing groups, or between the protesters and law
enforcement personnel or other government representatives.
B. Any member who believes that there is a threat of violence to personnel at any incident
shall promptly relay that information to the appropriate supervisor as quickly as possible.
C. The Incident Commander (IC), scene supervisor or senior ranking member has the
authority to initiate a tactical withdrawal and the responsibility for ensuring that all
members on-scene or at risk due to the threat are notified of the action. Authority for the
decision resides primarily with on- scene personnel and should not be delayed while
seeking approval or confirmation from a higher authority, who may not be at the incident
scene.
D. In the event that a credible threat to personnel is discovered at a level of the incident
command structure above an on-scene supervisor, a tactical withdrawal may be ordered
and relayed down the chain of command to the on-scene supervisor. In that event, the
supervisor has the responsibility for ensuring that all members on-scene or at risk due to
the threat are notified of the initiation of a tactical withdrawal.
II. WITHDRAWAL GUIDELINES
A. The following guidelines shall be applied when the decision has been made to initiate a
tactical withdrawal:
1. During the response to an incident:
a) If a tactical withdrawal occurs during the response phase of an incident,
the department member responsible for initiating the withdrawal is
responsible for notifying all responding units and Dispatch of the
withdrawal action.
b) The relay of the withdrawal decision to individual units may be conducted
by the member, or he/she may choose to have Dispatch notify all
responding units to cancel their response or to respond to a defined
staging area.
2. After arrival at an incident:
a) When units are on-scene at an incident and a decision is made to initiate
a tactical withdrawal, the IC or ranking supervisor is responsible for
notifying all involved units (including those assigned to the incident but
that have not yet arrived) of the withdrawal action.
b) The IC shall also notify Dispatch of the tactical withdrawal, and if time and
circumstances allow, the situation and reason for the withdrawal.
c) Individual unit supervisors are responsible for notifying all of their
assigned personnel of the withdrawal.

B. The following guidelines shall be applied when the decision has been made to initiate a
tactical withdrawal:
1. Whenever a tactical withdrawal is initiated, a defined staging area will be
established at a safe location away from the incident scene and all involved units
and personnel should withdraw to that staging area. Whenever practicable, all
involved units should withdraw from the incident scene as a single group. If that
is not practicable, individual units should attempt to congregate together,
forming the fewest and largest groups practicable, and withdraw in those groups.
2. After all units have been initially notified of a tactical withdrawal, individual unit
supervisors are responsible for personnel accountability, ensuring all members of
their crew are accounted for and withdrawing as directed. The on-scene
supervisor is responsible for accounting for all units assigned to the call and
ensuring that all units are withdrawing as directed.
3. Whenever a tactical withdrawal is initiated, Dispatch shall immediately notify and
request an immediate response by the appropriate law enforcement agency to
provide security for the withdrawing units.
4. Once the IC or scene supervisor believes that all units and personnel have
withdrawn from an incident, he/she shall conduct a Personnel Accountability
Report (PAR) of all units assigned to the incident to confirm they have safely
withdrawn. Individual unit supervisors shall confirm that all members of their
crew are accounted for and safe.
5. Once all involved units have gathered at the staging area, the IC or scene
supervisor shall again conduct a PAR to confirm that all personnel are safe. If any
person involved in the operation is unaccounted for, emergency procedures shall
be initiated.
III. PATIENT CARE CONSIDERATIONS
A. Special consideration shall be taken when a tactical withdrawal is initiated after members
have begun providing medical assessment or medical care at an incident scene. If a
tactical withdrawal is initiated at a time that members are providing medical services to
sick or injured patients, those members should, whenever practicable, attempt to
maintain their care of medical patients and evacuate those patients as part of the
withdrawal process.
B. In the event that violence or the threat of violence forces members to abandon any
patient under their care, the involved member shall immediately notify the appropriate
law enforcement agency of the location of the patient and request immediate assistance
in securing the scene to allow for safe and timely medical treatment and evacuation of
the patient. The members shall remain on the call and wait for law enforcement clearance
or other information indicating that it is safe to enter the incident scene. Once it is safe
to do so, the members shall attempt to locate the patient and resume medical evaluation,
treatment and transport per protocol. In the event that law enforcement personnel and
department members are unable to relocate the patient, the patient may be deemed to
have self-extracted and the appropriate documentation shall be prepared.

IV. NOTIFICATIONS
A. Whenever a tactical withdrawal is initiated, the circumstances of the incident, including
the incident location, will be relayed up the chain of command to the on-duty Officer in
Charge. The Officer in Charge shall ensure that all Operations Division personnel are
immediately notified of the location and circumstances of the incident.
B. The Officer in Charge shall coordinate with Dispatch and law enforcement to ensure
additional calls for service to the affected area are screened and determined safe for
entry.
By Order of:
Jeff Boyajian
Fire Chief

title: Aircraft Operations
body:
PURPOSE:
This policy describes standards for the safe operation of firefighting and medical evacuation aircraft that
may be working with ground personnel at any incident involving the tactical use of aircraft.
POLICY:
The Stickney Fire Department will follow Incident Command System (ICS) standards for managing
firefighting aircraft operations, including the identification, establishment and management of aircraft
landing zones, any time that firefighting or medical evacuation aircraft are in tactical use at any emergency
incident.
I. AUTHORITY
A. The authority to call for assistance that would include a helicopter lies with the Incident
Commander.
B. A helicopter may be called when the Incident Commander has information from medical
personnel on the scene that one or more patients meet the criteria for air transport as
established by the Project Medical Director.
C. A helicopter may be called when instructed to by the resource hospital.
D. A helicopter can be placed on “Standby” by the Incident Commander at any time at
his/her discretion prior to notifying the resource hospital.
II. RESPONSIBILITIES
A. Upon determining the need for a helicopter, the Incident Commander shall notify
Communications of the request. The Incident Commander shall give Communications the
incident type; the incident location; the number of patients; and an assigned radio
frequency. Do not ask Communications for wind direction or speed unless the helicopter
is landing at Communications.
B. After requesting a helicopter, the Incident Commander shall assign a Landing Zone Officer
(LZO). The Landing Zone Officer shall be responsible for establishing a safe landing zone
and communicating landing information to the flight crew. The Incident Commander shall
provide the Landing Zone Officer with sufficient personnel to establish a safe Landing
Zone.

C. The Landing Zone Officer shall maintain an accurate timeline of activities. The Landing
Zone Officer shall also provide updates of patient information to the flight crew.
D. The Landing Zone Officer shall then assign a Tail Rotor Observer whose responsibility shall
be to protect against and prevent personnel from approaching the aircraft from the rear.
E. Both the Landing Zone Officer and the Tail Rotor Observer shall be identified using a
Sector Officer vest. Neither the Landing Zone Officer nor the Tail Rotor Observer shall act
as or replace the Incident Safety Officer.
F. No other assignments shall be given to either the Landing Zone Officer or Tail Rotor
Observer until the helicopter operation is completed in full and the helicopter has lifted
off. The Landing Zone Officer and Tail Rotor Observer shall remain at the Landing Zone
until the conclusion of the take-off.
G. The Landing Zone Officer and the Tail Rotor Observer shall have the authority and
responsibility to cancel or modify the air/ground operation at any time when either
deems the operation unsafe.
III. COMMUNICATIONS
A. All communications between the Incident Commander and the Landing Zone Officer shall
be on a fireground frequency selected by the IC. Communications between the Landing
Zone Officer and the medical personnel shall use a separate frequency such as a
secondary fireground or MERCI frequency.
B. All communications between the helicopter and the ground shall be with the Landing
Zone Officer only. The Landing Zone Officer shall communicate with the helicopter using
the IREACH frequency or an available MERCI channel.
C. Typically, communications will cease when the pilot has completed at least one fly over
to determine the landing site and approximately 1 minute prior to touch down. Any
communication during the final approach should be initiated by the pilot except in an
emergency and then the emergency should be declared by the Landing Zone Officer by
repeating “Go Around” three (3) times. Air-to-ground communication capability should
be maintained while the helicopter is on the ground and for at least 2-3 minutes after
take-off.
D. Communications between the Landing Zone Officer and the Tail Rotor Observer should
normally be by visual hand signals or by radio using the fireground frequency.
E. IFERN or other MABAS radio channels are not an acceptable alternative and, if used by
the aircraft, the pilot should be instructed by the Landing Zone Officer as to which channel
to use.
IV. ESTABLISHING A LANDING ZONE (LZ)
A. The selection of a Landing Zone is critically important and shall be made by the Landing
Zone Officer.
B. The Landing Zone must be a relatively flat surface free of obstructions and debris
measuring at least 100’ x 100’ for each helicopter used. The Landing Zone should be
approachable into the wind. Approach and departure paths should not be over the
incident. The selected Landing Zone shall be accessible by ambulance and does not
necessarily need to be adjacent to the incident. A remote area is often safer for both the
flight crew as well as ground personnel.

C. The Landing Zone shall be clearly marked by using marker cones, marker lights, flags,
vehicles or other easily identifiable markers and then described to the pilot along with
any possible hazards.
D. If a roadway is used for a Landing Zone, the roadway shall be closed to all traffic for 300
feet in each direction. The police department should be made aware of distances required
when seeking assistance to close a roadway; be specific, using identifiable markers or
cross streets when available.
E. Spectators and non-essential personnel should be kept back from the Landing Zone at
least 200 feet.
V. OPERATING AROUND THE HELICOPTER
A. All approaches shall be done from the front of the aircraft after the pilot has signaled that
it is safe to do so. Approaches should be made from the downhill side if the Landing Zone
is on a sloping grade and should be made in a crouching position. NEVER APPROACH AN
AIRCRAFT FROM THE REAR. STAY CLEAR OF THE TAIL ROTOR.
B. Fire department personnel shall not operate or attempt to operate any equipment,
mechanical devices or doors of the aircraft.
C. Fire department personnel shall only assist the flight crew in the loading of the patient
and stretcher unless specifically instructed to do so by the flight crew.
D. Fire department personnel shall immediately leave the Landing Zone after completing the
patient transfer and loading.
VI. PERSONNEL PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT
A. Personnel Protective Equipment (PPE) shall be utilized by all personnel while operating at
the incident.
B. When operating at or near the Landing Zone, all personnel shall wear a turnout coat and
pants, gloves, eye shields and a helmet with the chin strap securely fastened. Hearing
protection should be used when available.
VII. SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS
A. Personnel shall not run near the Landing Zone. Vehicles shall not be parked closer than
100’ to the Landing Zone
B. Approaching the aircraft from the rear is strictly prohibited.
C. Talking to, mingling with or distracting the Tail Rotor Observer is prohibited.
D. Items used to mark the Landing Zone should be weighted or securely fasten to the ground.
E. Always be mindful of rotor wash; never chase anything that is blown around or onto the
Landing Zone.
F. All distances should be increased 20% for night-time operation.
G. Avoid using flood lights unless to illuminate a hazard, in which case the light should be
shining to the ground to where the hazard is located.
H. Take-offs and landings are generally not vertical, allow for upwind approach paths.
I. Cross winds generally should not be greater than 45 degrees.

J. Do not use police officers for Landing Zone operations.
VIII. TERMINATION
A. The Landing Zone Officer shall notify the Incident Commander upon take-off of the
helicopter. The Landing Zone Officer shall stand-down all personnel involved and shall
make certain that the Landing Zone is returned to its previous condition and document
any damage.
B. After the Landing Zone is restored, all remaining personnel shall report to the Incident
Commander for re-assignment.
By Order of:
Jeff Boyajian
Fire Chief

title: Atmospheric Monitoring For Carbon Monoxide
body:
PURPOSE:
This policy establishes procedures for measuring atmospheric concentrations of carbon monoxide (CO) at
an incident for the safety of members working in potentially hazardous conditions.
POLICY:
Exposure to CO can be hazardous to the health of those exposed. It is the policy of the Stickney Fire
Department to mitigate the health risks associated with exposure to CO by its members and the public.
I. DEFINITIONS
A. Calibration - The process of resetting the values for each sensor in the instrument.
B. Spanning - The process of using the calibration gasses to check the calibration of the
instrument, also known as bump testing.
II. RESPONSIBILITIES
A. Officer in Charge or acting officer should ensure that atmospheric monitoring instruments
are bump tested or calibrated to manufacturer’s specifications on a daily basis during the
1800 to 0600 shift.
B. The instruments should be stored in operating condition.
C. The Officer in Charge/acting officer or the authorized designee is responsible for
measuring atmospheric concentrations of CO at any location containing or suspected of
containing elevated levels of CO.
III. PROCEDURES
A. Carbon monoxide may be present as a by-product of combustion, an emission from
internal combustion engines, a chemical reaction or a leak from an industrial process.
Carbon monoxide has approximately the same vapor density as air. When measuring for
atmospheric concentrations of CO at an incident, instruments do not have to be placed
near the floor or ceiling to obtain accurate readings.
B. Positive pressure ventilation may be used to reduce the CO concentration, as well as the
presence of other toxic gases in the atmosphere.

C. All members shall use self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA) in any atmosphere
containing 35 parts per million or greater of CO. An atmospheric concentration of CO that
is below 35 parts per million does not necessarily indicate an adequate level of oxygen or
eliminate the possibility of other toxic gases or products of combustion being present.
D. Members shall also use an SCBA in any atmospheric concentration of CO that is below 35
parts per million where there is also the presence of visible smoke, and in any atmosphere
containing less than 19.5 percent oxygen (820 ILCS 219/25; 29 CFR 1910.134).
IV. EMERGENCY MEDICAL TREATMENT
A. A person with acute CO exposure may exhibit the signs and symptoms of headache,
flushing, nausea, vertigo, weakness, irritability, unconsciousness, and in persons with preexisting heart disease and atherosclerosis, chest pain and leg pain.
B. An affected or incapacitated person should be removed from further exposure and have
appropriate emergency medical procedures implemented, including any listed on the
Safety Data Sheet (SDS) for CO. (See Policy 910 - HAZARD COMMUNICATION)
C. All personnel with the potential for becoming exposed to CO or being present during an
exposure should be familiar with emergency procedures, the location and proper use of
emergency equipment, and the methods of protecting themselves during rescue
operations.
By Order Of:
Jeff Boyajian
Fire Chief
